stem: Light from a point source reaches the Earth from a very distant star. Over a small region near the Earth, the wavefront is
explanation: A point source gives spherical wavefronts, but at a very large distance the radius is so large that a small part of the sphere is practically flat, so the wavefront is plane. Spherical is the shape close to the source, not far away.

stem: According to Huygens' principle, each point on a wavefront
options: reflects the wave back towards the source
acts as a source of secondary wavelets
explanation: Huygens' principle says every point of a wavefront behaves as a source of secondary spherical wavelets; the new wavefront is the surface tangent to these wavelets after a time t. It says nothing about points absorbing or reflecting the wave.

stem: The direction of propagation of light (a ray) is always
options: along the tangent to the wavefront
explanation: A ray shows the direction in which the wave energy travels, and it is always normal (at 90°) to the wavefront. A ray along the wavefront or tangent to it would mean the wave moves sideways along its own surface of constant phase, which does not happen.

stem: Two points P and Q lie on the same wavefront of a light wave. The phase difference between the vibrations at P and Q is
explanation: A wavefront is defined as the locus of all points vibrating in the same phase, so any two points on it have zero phase difference. A phase difference of π would hold for points half a wavelength apart along the ray, not on one wavefront.

stem: A long, narrow illuminated slit acts as a line source of light. Close to the slit, the wavefronts it produces are
explanation: Every point of a line source sends out wavelets, and together they form surfaces of equal distance from the line, which are cylinders with the slit as axis. Spherical wavefronts come from a point source, and plane wavefronts appear only very far from the source.

stem: Two light sources are said to be coherent if they
options: have exactly the same intensity only
explanation: Coherent sources keep a constant phase difference, which requires the same frequency (wavelength); only then does a steady interference pattern form. Equal intensity or amplitude alone is not enough, because two separate lamps of equal brightness still change phase randomly.

stem: In Young's double slit experiment, with slit separation d, screen distance L and wavelength λ, the fringe spacing is
explanation: Bright fringes lie at y = mλL/d, so neighbouring fringes are separated by Δy = λL/d. Writing λd/L inverts the role of d and L: a larger slit separation actually brings the fringes closer together.

stem: In Young's double slit experiment, light of wavelength 600 nm falls on slits 0.3 mm apart and the screen is 1.5 m away. The fringe spacing is
explanation: Δy = λL/d = (600 × 10⁻⁹ × 1.5)/(0.3 × 10⁻³) = 3 × 10⁻³ m = 3 mm. The value 6 mm comes from using half the slit separation, as if d were measured from the centre line.

stem: In Young's experiment, the slit separation is doubled and the distance to the screen is halved, with the same light. The fringe spacing becomes
explanation: Δy = λL/d. Halving L halves Δy and doubling d halves it again, so Δy becomes (1/2)(1/2) = 1/4 of the original. Thinking the two changes cancel gives unchanged, but both act in the same direction.

stem: In a Young's double slit set-up, the fringe spacing is 2.0 mm with light of wavelength 500 nm. If the light is changed to wavelength 600 nm and nothing else changes, the fringe spacing becomes
explanation: Δy is proportional to λ, so Δy = 2.0 × 600/500 = 2.4 mm. The value 1.67 mm uses the inverse ratio 500/600, as if a longer wavelength gave narrower fringes.

stem: In Young's experiment, λ = 500 nm, the slit separation is 0.5 mm and the screen is 1 m away. The distance of the third dark fringe from the centre of the pattern is
explanation: λL/d = (500 × 10⁻⁹ × 1)/(0.5 × 10⁻³) = 1 mm. Dark fringes lie at (m + ½)λL/d, and the third dark fringe has m = 2, so y = 2.5 × 1 mm = 2.5 mm. The value 3 mm is the third bright fringe, and 3.5 mm would be the fourth dark fringe.

stem: A complete Young's double slit apparatus is moved from air into water of refractive index 4/3. The fringe spacing
explanation: In water the wavelength becomes λ/n = 3λ/4 while d and L are unchanged, so Δy = λL/d becomes 3/4 of its value in air. Choosing 4/3 multiplies by n instead of dividing; light slows down and its wavelength shortens in water.

stem: Young's double slit experiment is performed with white light. The central fringe is
explanation: At the centre the path difference is zero for every wavelength, so all colours interfere constructively there and the central fringe is white. Coloured fringes appear only away from the centre, where different wavelengths have their maxima at different places.

stem: In Young's experiment with light of wavelength 600 nm, the path difference between the waves reaching a point P on the screen is 1.5 μm. At P there is the
explanation: Path difference/λ = 1.5 μm/0.6 μm = 2.5, an odd number of half wavelengths, so the point is dark. Dark fringes occur at path differences 0.5λ, 1.5λ and 2.5λ, so this is the third dark fringe. Calling it the second dark fringe starts the count at 1.5λ and misses the dark fringe next to the centre.

stem: In a Young's double slit experiment, the slits are 2 mm apart and the screen is 2 m away. A span of 10 fringe widths on the screen measures 6 mm. The wavelength of the light is
explanation: One fringe width is 6/10 = 0.6 mm, and λ = Δy d/L = (0.6 × 10⁻³ × 2 × 10⁻³)/2 = 6 × 10⁻⁷ m = 600 nm. The value 667 nm comes from dividing 6 mm by 9, as if the 10 fringes enclosed only 9 widths.

stem: In a Young's double slit experiment, two wavelengths are used together. The third bright fringe of light of wavelength 600 nm falls exactly on the fourth bright fringe of the second light. The second wavelength is
explanation: Bright fringes lie at y = mλL/d, so coincidence needs 3 × 600 = 4 × λ₂, giving λ₂ = 1800/4 = 450 nm. The value 800 nm comes from writing 4 × 600 = 3λ₂, which swaps the fringe orders.

stem: In Young's experiment, either slit alone gives an intensity I at the centre of the screen. With both slits open and the light coherent, the intensity at the central bright fringe is
explanation: At the central maximum the two waves arrive in phase, so the amplitudes add to 2A, and intensity, being proportional to amplitude squared, becomes 4I. The value 2I adds intensities, which is correct only for incoherent light.

stem: Two identical bulbs placed side by side do not produce an interference pattern on a wall because
explanation: Light from two separate bulbs is emitted by independent atoms whose phases change randomly many millions of times a second, so the phase difference is not constant and any pattern washes out. Brightness, wavelength and speed do not stop interference.

stem: The bright colours seen on a thin soap film in sunlight are due to
explanation: Light reflected from the front and back surfaces of the film interferes; for each thickness some wavelengths reinforce and others cancel, giving colours. Dispersion by a prism also gives colours, but the soap film has no prism action and the colours change with thickness.

stem: When light travelling in air is reflected from the surface of glass, the reflected wave undergoes a phase change of
explanation: Reflection at the boundary with an optically denser medium produces a phase change of π, equivalent to an extra path of λ/2. Reflection from a rarer medium (glass to air inside the glass) gives no phase change, so 'zero' is the case for the other direction.

stem: A thin film of refractive index 1.5 is surrounded by air and is lit normally by light of wavelength 600 nm. The minimum thickness for which the film looks bright in reflected light is
explanation: Reflection from the top surface has a π phase change and from the bottom surface none, so brightness needs 2nt = λ/2, giving t = λ/(4n) = 600/(4 × 1.5) = 100 nm. The value 200 nm comes from 2nt = λ, which ignores the phase change.

stem: A soap film in air becomes extremely thin (much thinner than the wavelength of light) just before it bursts. In reflected light it then appears
explanation: For thickness close to zero the path difference 2nt is negligible, but the wave reflected from the front surface has an extra phase change of π, so the two reflected waves cancel and the film looks dark. Without the phase change one would wrongly expect constructive interference and a white film.

stem: A thin oil film of refractive index 1.25 floats on water of refractive index 1.33. For normal incidence, the minimum non-zero thickness of oil that strongly reflects light of wavelength 500 nm is
explanation: Both reflections (air to oil, oil to water) are from a denser medium, so both have a π change and they cancel out. Constructive reflection then needs 2nt = λ, so t = 500/(2 × 1.25) = 200 nm. The value 100 nm, λ/(4n), wrongly applies the rule for a film with air on both sides.

stem: In thin film interference seen in reflected light, the interfering waves are the waves reflected from
options: the top and bottom faces of the film
only the upper surface of the film
two separate lamps placed near the film
only the lower surface of the film
explanation: Part of the light reflects from the top surface and part enters, reflects from the bottom surface and comes back out; these two coherent parts interfere. A single reflected wave cannot interfere with itself to produce colours.

stem: A lens is coated with a thin layer of refractive index 1.38 (the glass has index 1.5) to reduce reflection of light of wavelength 552 nm at normal incidence. The minimum thickness of the coating is
explanation: Both reflections (air to coating, coating to glass) have a π phase change, so cancellation needs 2nt = λ/2, giving t = λ/(4n) = 552/(4 × 1.38) = 100 nm. The value 138 nm is λ/4 without dividing by n; the wavelength inside the coating is shorter.

stem: In the Newton's rings arrangement, a convex lens rests on a flat glass plate. The thin film whose interference produces the rings is
options: a glass film inside the lens
an oil film spread over the lens surface
an air film between lens and plate
a water film below the plate
explanation: The curved lens surface and the flat plate enclose a wedge-shaped air film whose thickness grows from zero at the point of contact. Light reflected from the top and bottom of this air film interferes and gives the rings. No oil or water is used in the standard arrangement.

stem: Newton's rings are viewed in reflected monochromatic light. The central spot, at the point where the lens touches the plate, is
explanation: At the point of contact the air film has zero thickness, but the wave reflected from the glass plate has an extra phase change of π, so the two reflected waves cancel and the centre is dark. Ignoring this phase change would wrongly predict a bright centre.

stem: The fringes in the Newton's rings experiment are circular because
options: the lamp used has a circular shape
the lens absorbs some of the light along circular zones
the plate is polished in circular strokes
the air film thickness is constant along circles
explanation: Each fringe is a locus of equal film thickness. The air gap below a spherical lens has the same thickness at all points equidistant from the point of contact, that is, along circles. The shape of the lamp has no effect on the fringe shape.

stem: In a Newton's rings experiment, the air between the lens and the plate is replaced by water. The rings
explanation: The condition for a given ring is 2nt = mλ; with water (n = 4/3) the same m is reached at a smaller thickness t, which lies closer to the centre, so the rings shrink. Expecting larger rings treats the higher refractive index as if it lengthened the wavelength.

stem: In Newton's rings seen in reflected light, the radius of a dark ring is proportional to the square root of its order. The ratio of the radius of the 1st dark ring to that of the 4th dark ring is
explanation: Since r ∝ √n, r₁/r₄ = √1/√4 = 1/2, so the ratio is 1:2. The ratio 1:4 takes r proportional to n itself, forgetting the square root.

stem: Newton's rings are formed in reflected light of wavelength 600 nm, with an air film. Counting the central dark spot as order zero, the thickness of the air film at the 5th dark ring is
explanation: With the π phase change at the lower surface, dark rings occur where 2t = mλ, so for m = 5, t = 5 × 600/2 = 1500 nm = 1.5 μm. The value 3.0 μm forgets that the light crosses the film twice, and 1.65 μm uses the bright-ring condition (m + ½)λ.

stem: In a Michelson interferometer, the incoming beam of light is divided into two beams by
explanation: A half-silvered plate (beam splitter) reflects about half the light towards one mirror and transmits the other half to the second mirror, giving two coherent beams. A prism would disperse the light rather than split it into two equal coherent parts.

stem: In a Michelson interferometer using light of wavelength 600 nm, the movable mirror is moved through 0.15 mm. The number of fringes that pass the reference mark is
explanation: Each fringe shift corresponds to a mirror movement of λ/2, so m = 2d/λ = (2 × 0.15 × 10⁻³)/(600 × 10⁻⁹) = 500. The value 250 uses m = d/λ, forgetting that the light travels to the mirror and back.

stem: In a Michelson interferometer, the movable mirror is moved through a distance of λ/4. The fringe pattern shifts by
explanation: Moving the mirror by λ/4 changes the path of that beam by 2 × λ/4 = λ/2, which shifts the pattern by half a fringe, so a bright fringe is replaced by a dark one. One fringe needs a path change of λ, that is, a mirror movement of λ/2.

stem: When the movable mirror of a Michelson interferometer is moved through 0.29 mm, 1000 fringes cross the field of view. The wavelength of the light is
explanation: 2d = mλ gives λ = 2d/m = (2 × 0.29 × 10⁻³)/1000 = 5.8 × 10⁻⁷ m = 580 nm. The value 290 nm uses λ = d/m, missing the factor 2 for the return path.

stem: A Michelson interferometer is mainly used to
options: find the focal length of a lens
find the critical angle of glass
find the magnifying power of a telescope
explanation: By counting fringes as the mirror moves a measured distance, the interferometer gives the wavelength of light (or very small lengths) with high precision. Focal lengths and critical angles are measured with simple ray optics, not interference.

stem: Diffraction of light through a slit is most noticeable when the width of the slit is
options: about the size of the wavelength
about a thousand times the wavelength
about a million times the wavelength
about the size of the screen
explanation: Spreading of light past an opening is significant only when the opening is comparable to the wavelength; for much wider openings the light travels on almost straight. This is why visible light (λ ≈ 500 nm) shows little diffraction through a door or window.

stem: Light of wavelength 600 nm falls normally on a single slit of width 1.2 μm. The angle of the first minimum from the central direction is
explanation: For a single slit, the first minimum is at a sin θ = λ, so sin θ = 0.6/1.2 = 0.5 and θ = 30°. The value 60° comes from using cos θ = 0.5.

stem: Light of wavelength 500 nm passes through a single slit of width 0.2 mm onto a screen 2 m away. The width of the central bright band is
explanation: The first minima lie at y = ±λL/a = ±(500 × 10⁻⁹ × 2)/(0.2 × 10⁻³) = ±5 mm, so the central band is 2 × 5 = 10 mm wide. The value 5 mm is only the distance from the centre to one minimum.

stem: In a single slit diffraction experiment, the slit is made narrower while the wavelength and screen distance stay the same. The central maximum
explanation: The angular half-width of the central maximum is given by sin θ = λ/a, so a smaller slit width a gives a larger θ and a wider central band. Expecting a narrower band treats the slit as an aperture that simply casts a smaller shadow image.

stem: In the single slit diffraction pattern, the width of the central maximum compared with the width of each secondary maximum is
explanation: Minima occur at sin θ = λ/a, 2λ/a, 3λ/a, … on both sides. The central maximum stretches from −λ/a to +λ/a, a width of 2λ/a, while each secondary maximum spans only λ/a, so the central one is twice as wide.

stem: Light of wavelength 600 nm passes through a single slit of width 0.1 mm. The angle between the first minima on the two sides of the central maximum is about
explanation: For small angles θ ≈ λ/a = (600 × 10⁻⁹)/(0.1 × 10⁻³) = 6 × 10⁻³ rad to each side, so the angle between the two first minima is 2θ = 1.2 × 10⁻² rad. The value 6 × 10⁻³ rad is the angle on one side only.

stem: In single slit diffraction, at a certain angle the path difference between the light from the two edges of the slit is 2λ. In this direction there is the
explanation: Minima occur where a sin θ = mλ; a path difference of 2λ between the edges gives m = 2, the second minimum. A path difference of 2λ would mean a bright fringe in a double slit, which is the tempting but wrong analogy.

stem: For a diffraction grating with grating element d, the condition for the nth order bright line of wavelength λ at angle θ is
explanation: Light from neighbouring slits of a grating reinforces when its path difference d sin θ is a whole number of wavelengths, so d sin θ = nλ. The cosine form would give the maximum light at θ = 90°, which is not observed.

stem: A diffraction grating has 5000 lines per centimetre. Its grating element is
explanation: d = 1/(5000 per cm) = 2 × 10⁻⁴ cm = 2 × 10⁻⁶ m = 2 μm. The value 0.2 μm comes from treating the figure as lines per millimetre.

stem: A grating with 5000 lines per centimetre is lit normally by light of wavelength 500 nm. The angle of the second-order maximum is
explanation: d = 2 μm, so sin θ = nλ/d = (2 × 0.5)/2 = 0.5 and θ = 30°. The value 15° halves the angle for the first order, but sin θ, not θ, is proportional to n.

stem: A grating with grating element 2 μm is lit normally by light of wavelength 450 nm. The highest order of maximum that can be seen is
explanation: Since sin θ cannot exceed 1, n ≤ d/λ = 2000/450 ≈ 4.4, so the highest whole order is 4. Rounding 4.4 up to 5 would need sin θ greater than 1, which is impossible.

stem: Light of wavelength 500 nm falls normally on a diffraction grating, and the first-order maximum appears at 30°. The number of lines per millimetre on the grating is
explanation: d = nλ/sin θ = 500 nm/0.5 = 1000 nm = 10⁻³ mm, so there are 1/10⁻³ = 1000 lines per mm. The value 2000 comes from taking d = λ = 500 nm, which forgets to divide by sin θ.

stem: A grating is lit by light containing wavelengths 400 nm and 600 nm. The third-order maximum of the 400 nm light falls at the same angle as which order of the 600 nm light?
explanation: Same angle means the same d sin θ, so 3 × 400 = n × 600, giving n = 2. Choosing the third order assumes equal orders always overlap, which happens only for equal wavelengths.

stem: The fact that light can be polarised shows that light waves are
explanation: Polarisation means restricting the vibrations to one plane perpendicular to the direction of travel, which is possible only for transverse waves. Longitudinal waves such as sound vibrate along the direction of travel and cannot be polarised.

stem: Sound waves in air cannot be polarised because they are
explanation: In a longitudinal wave the particles vibrate along the direction of travel, so there is no sideways vibration that a polariser could select. Speed or wavelength has nothing to do with it: long radio waves can still be polarised because they are transverse.

stem: Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ falls on an ideal polaroid sheet. The intensity of the transmitted light is
explanation: Unpolarised light has vibrations equally in all directions, and a polaroid passes only the component along its axis; averaging cos²θ over all directions gives 1/2, so I = I₀/2. Taking I₀ assumes the polaroid lets all light through, which happens only for light already polarised along its axis.

stem: Unpolarised light passes through two ideal polaroids whose transmission axes are perpendicular to each other. The intensity of light coming out of the second polaroid is
explanation: The first polaroid passes light vibrating along its own axis; the second polaroid, with its axis at 90°, has no component of that vibration to pass (cos² 90° = 0), so no light emerges. One-half is the intensity after the first sheet only.

stem: Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ passes through a polariser and then an analyser whose axis makes 60° with that of the polariser. The final intensity is (use Malus's law I = I₁ cos² θ)
explanation: After the polariser I₁ = I₀/2. Then I = I₁ cos² 60° = (I₀/2)(1/4) = I₀/8. The value 3I₀/8 uses sin² 60° = 3/4 instead of cos² 60°, and I₀/4 forgets that the first sheet already halves the intensity.

stem: Light reflected from a glass surface of refractive index √3 is completely plane polarised when the angle of incidence θ satisfies tan θ = n. This angle is
explanation: tan θ = √3 gives θ = 60°, the polarising (Brewster) angle; at this angle the reflected and refracted rays are at 90° to each other. The value 30° is the angle whose tangent is 1/√3, obtained by inverting n.

stem: Which of the following waves cannot be polarised?
explanation: Ultrasound in air is a sound wave, which is longitudinal, so it cannot be polarised. Radio waves, X-rays and light are all electromagnetic waves, which are transverse and can be polarised even though some of them are invisible.

stem: Polaroid sunglasses reduce the glare of sunlight reflected from a wet road mainly because the reflected light is
explanation: Light reflected from a horizontal surface is partly polarised with its vibrations mostly horizontal; the polaroid lenses have vertical transmission axes and block much of it. Reflection does not change the wavelength, and coherence has nothing to do with glare.

stem: Plane polarised light is passed through each of the following. Which one rotates the plane of polarisation?
explanation: A sugar solution is optically active: it rotates the plane of polarisation by an angle depending on its concentration, which is used to measure sugar content. Pure water and ordinary glass are not optically active and leave the plane unchanged.

stem: An object 2 cm tall forms an image 6 cm tall through a lens. The linear magnification is
explanation: Linear magnification = image height/object height = 6/2 = 3. The value 1/3 divides the other way round, object height by image height.

stem: The angular magnification (magnifying power) of an optical instrument is defined as the ratio of the
options: image height to object height, both measured on a screen
image distance to object distance, both measured from the lens
focal length of the objective to the focal length of the eyepiece
angle at the eye due to the image to that due to the object
explanation: Magnifying power M = θ′/θ, where θ′ is the angle subtended at the eye by the image and θ is the angle subtended by the object when seen directly (at the near point for a microscope). Image height over object height is the linear magnification, a different quantity.

stem: The least distance of distinct vision (near point) for a normal adult eye is taken as
explanation: A normal eye can focus clearly on objects from about 25 cm out to infinity, so d = 25 cm is used in microscope formulas. Objects held nearer than this look blurred.

stem: An object is placed 30 cm from a converging lens of focal length 20 cm. The magnification of the real image formed is
explanation: 1/q = 1/f − 1/p = 1/20 − 1/30 = 1/60, so q = 60 cm and M = q/p = 60/30 = 2. The value 1.5 is p/f, which is not a magnification, and 0.5 is p/q, the ratio inverted.

stem: In a simple microscope (magnifying glass), the object is placed
options: between F and 2F of the lens
explanation: A convex lens forms a virtual, erect, magnified image only when the object is inside its focal length, between the lens and F. Objects beyond F give real, inverted images, as in a projector or camera.

stem: A convex lens of focal length 5 cm is used as a simple microscope with the final image at the near point (25 cm). Its magnifying power is
explanation: M = 1 + d/f = 1 + 25/5 = 6. The value 5 is d/f, which is correct only when the image is formed at infinity, not at the near point.

stem: A simple microscope must give a magnifying power of 11 with the final image at the near point (25 cm). The focal length of the lens should be
explanation: From M = 1 + d/f, 11 = 1 + 25/f gives f = 25/10 = 2.5 cm. The value 2.27 cm uses M = d/f (25/11), the formula for an image at infinity.

stem: A lens of power +10 dioptres is used as a magnifying glass, with the final image at the near point (25 cm). The magnifying power is
explanation: f = 1/P = 1/10 m = 10 cm, so M = 1 + d/f = 1 + 25/10 = 3.5. The value 2.5 is d/f, the result for an image at infinity.

stem: The image formed by a simple microscope is
explanation: With the object inside the focal length of a convex lens, the rays leave diverging and appear to come from a virtual, upright, enlarged image on the same side as the object. A real, inverted image needs the object beyond F.

stem: Which statement about a compound microscope is correct?
options: The eyepiece has the shorter focal length
The objective has a shorter focal length
The objective is a concave lens
explanation: Both lenses are convex; the objective has a very short focal length so the object can be placed just outside its focus and give a large real image, which the eyepiece then magnifies. In a telescope, by contrast, the objective has the longer focal length.

stem: Compared with the object, the final image seen in a compound microscope is
explanation: The objective forms a real, inverted, magnified image; the eyepiece acts as a magnifier on it and gives a virtual image without inverting it again. So the final image is virtual, inverted relative to the object and magnified. It is not real, because no screen can catch it.

stem: In a compound microscope, the objective produces a linear magnification of 10 and the eyepiece a magnification of 5. The total magnification is
explanation: The eyepiece magnifies the image already magnified by the objective, so the total is the product, 10 × 5 = 50. Adding them to get 15 treats the lenses as working side by side instead of one after the other.

stem: In a compound microscope, the objective (f = 1 cm) has the object 1.25 cm in front of it. The eyepiece (f = 5 cm) forms the final image at the near point, 25 cm. The magnifying power is
explanation: Objective: 1/q = 1/1 − 1/1.25 = 0.2, so q = 5 cm and M₀ = q/p = 5/1.25 = 4. Eyepiece: Mₑ = 1 + 25/5 = 6. Total M = 4 × 6 = 24. The value 20 takes Mₑ = 25/5 = 5, the result for a final image at infinity.

stem: To increase the magnifying power of a compound microscope, one should use
options: an objective and an eyepiece of short focal length
an objective and an eyepiece of long focal length
an objective of long and an eyepiece of short focal length
a concave lens as the eyepiece
explanation: M ≈ (L/f₀)(1 + d/fₑ), so a smaller f₀ and a smaller fₑ each increase M. A long-focus objective with a short-focus eyepiece describes a telescope, where M = f₀/fₑ.

stem: An astronomical telescope has an objective of focal length 100 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm. In normal adjustment its magnifying power is
explanation: M = f₀/fₑ = 100/5 = 20. The value 105 cm is f₀ + fₑ, which is the length of the telescope, not its magnifying power.

stem: An astronomical telescope in normal adjustment has a magnifying power of 15 and an objective of focal length 90 cm. The distance between the objective and the eyepiece is
explanation: fₑ = f₀/M = 90/15 = 6 cm, and in normal adjustment the lens separation is f₀ + fₑ = 90 + 6 = 96 cm. The value 84 cm subtracts the focal lengths instead of adding them.

stem: The objective of a good astronomical telescope has
options: a long focal length and a large aperture
a short focal length and a small aperture
a long focal length and a small aperture
a short focal length and a large aperture
explanation: A long focal length gives a high magnifying power f₀/fₑ, and a large aperture collects more light and improves the resolving power. A short focal length objective belongs to a microscope.

stem: A telescope objective has a diameter of 0.122 m. For light of wavelength 500 nm, the smallest angular separation it can resolve (Rayleigh criterion θ = 1.22λ/D) is
explanation: θ = 1.22 × 500 × 10⁻⁹/0.122 = 1.22 × 5 × 10⁻⁷/0.122 = 5 × 10⁻⁶ rad. The value 4.1 × 10⁻⁶ rad drops the factor 1.22, which applies to a circular aperture.

stem: The resolving power of a telescope can be increased by
options: using an eyepiece of shorter focal length
using an objective of larger diameter
explanation: The smallest resolvable angle is θ = 1.22λ/D, so a larger objective diameter D (or a shorter wavelength) improves resolving power. A shorter-focus eyepiece only increases magnification; it enlarges a blurred image without separating close objects.

stem: An optical fibre has a core of refractive index 1.60 and a cladding of refractive index 0.8√3 (about 1.39). The critical angle at the core-cladding boundary is
explanation: sin C = n₂/n₁ = 0.8√3/1.6 = √3/2, so C = 60°. Light hitting the boundary at more than 60° to the normal is totally internally reflected. The value 30° comes from reading √3/2 as the cosine instead of the sine.

stem: Light travels along the axis of a straight optical fibre whose core has refractive index 1.5. Take c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s. The time taken to travel 1 km of fibre is
explanation: v = c/n = 3 × 10⁸/1.5 = 2 × 10⁸ m/s, so t = 1000/(2 × 10⁸) = 5 × 10⁻⁶ s = 5 μs. The value 3.3 μs uses the speed of light in vacuum, ignoring the core's refractive index.

stem: A graded-index optical fibre reduces the spreading of light pulses (multipath dispersion) compared with a step-index multimode fibre because
options: longer-path rays travel faster in the outer, lower-index glass
the core absorbs every ray that is not along the axis
the cladding reflects only one colour and absorbs the others
the refractive index of the core is highest at its outer edges
explanation: In a graded-index fibre the refractive index falls from the centre outwards, so rays that zigzag far from the axis travel through lower-index glass at higher speed and arrive nearly together with the axial ray. The index is highest at the centre, not the edges, and the core does not absorb oblique rays.

stem: Huygens' principle is used mainly to find
options: the speed of light in vacuum
the new position of a wavefront
the mass of a light photon
the focal length of a mirror
explanation: Huygens' construction draws secondary wavelets from every point of a known wavefront; the surface touching them all after time t is the new wavefront. It is a geometric method and does not give the speed of light or photon properties.

stem: In Young's experiment, the slits are 1 mm apart, the screen is 2 m away and the fringe spacing is 1.1 mm. The wavelength of the light is
explanation: λ = Δy d/L = (1.1 × 10⁻³ × 1 × 10⁻³)/2 = 5.5 × 10⁻⁷ m = 550 nm. The value 1100 nm forgets to divide by the screen distance of 2 m.

stem: When an astronomical telescope is in normal adjustment, the final image is formed
options: at the near point of the eye
at the focus of the objective
explanation: In normal adjustment the objective's image lies at the focus of the eyepiece, so rays leave the eyepiece parallel and the final image is at infinity, which the relaxed eye views comfortably. The intermediate (first) image, not the final one, is at the focus of the objective.

stem: In Young's double slit experiment, the path difference between the two waves reaching a point on the screen is 3λ. The point lies on the
explanation: A path difference of a whole number of wavelengths, mλ, gives a bright fringe; m = 3 gives the third bright fringe counted from the central one (m = 0). Dark fringes need an odd number of half wavelengths, such as 2.5λ.

stem: A soap film of refractive index 4/3 in air is lit normally by light of wavelength 640 nm. The least thickness for which it looks bright in reflected light is
explanation: With a π phase change at the front surface only, brightness needs 2nt = λ/2, so t = λ/(4n) = 640/(4 × 4/3) = 640 × 3/16 = 120 nm. The value 160 nm is λ/4, which forgets that the wavelength inside the film is λ/n.

stem: Newton's rings and the colours of thin films are examples of interference produced by
explanation: In thin films and Newton's rings one beam is split at a surface into a reflected and a transmitted part, which share the amplitude; this is division of amplitude. Young's double slit, where two parts of one wavefront pass through two slits, is division of wavefront.

stem: In a Michelson interferometer with light of wavelength 500 nm, 200 fringes cross the field of view as the movable mirror is displaced. The mirror moved through
explanation: Each fringe corresponds to a mirror movement of λ/2, so d = mλ/2 = 200 × 500 nm/2 = 50 000 nm = 50 μm. The value 100 μm uses d = mλ, forgetting that the light covers the extra distance twice.

stem: In the diffraction pattern of a single slit, the central band is
options: as bright as each of the other bands
dark, with bright bands on either side
the narrowest band of the pattern
the brightest and the widest band
explanation: All parts of the slit send light in phase straight ahead, so the centre is brightest, and it spans from the first minimum on one side to the first on the other, twice the width of the other bands. A dark centre is never found for a single slit.

stem: A grating has 4000 lines per centimetre and is lit normally by light of wavelength 600 nm. For the second-order maximum, sin θ equals
explanation: d = 1/4000 cm = 2.5 μm, so sin θ = nλ/d = (2 × 0.6)/2.5 = 0.48. The value 0.24 is the first-order result.

stem: A polaroid sheet is slowly rotated through a full turn in front of a beam of light, and the transmitted intensity stays the same throughout. The incident beam is
explanation: Unpolarised light has vibrations equally in all directions, so a polaroid passes half of it in every orientation. Plane polarised light would go from bright to dark twice per turn, and partly polarised light would vary between a maximum and a non-zero minimum.

stem: A compound microscope has an objective of focal length 0.8 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm, and the final image is at the near point (25 cm). Using M = (L/f₀)(1 + d/fₑ), the length L needed for a magnifying power of 150 is
explanation: 1 + d/fₑ = 1 + 25/5 = 6, so L/f₀ = 150/6 = 25 and L = 25 × 0.8 = 20 cm. The value 24 cm uses d/fₑ = 5 instead of 6, giving L/f₀ = 30.

stem: Light is guided along an optical fibre by
explanation: Light in the core meets the boundary with the lower-index cladding at angles greater than the critical angle and is totally internally reflected again and again along the fibre. Dispersion is actually a drawback in fibres because it spreads pulses.

stem: The pupil of an eye has a diameter of 2 mm. Taking λ = 500 nm and the Rayleigh criterion θ = 1.22λ/D, the greatest distance at which two car headlights 1.22 m apart can just be seen as separate is
explanation: θ = 1.22 × 500 × 10⁻⁹/(2 × 10⁻³) = 3.05 × 10⁻⁴ rad. The distance is separation/θ = 1.22/(3.05 × 10⁻⁴) = 4000 m = 4 km. The value 8 km comes from using the pupil radius, 1 mm, in place of the diameter, which halves θ.

stem: A grating with grating element 2 μm is lit normally by light of wavelength 600 nm. The total number of bright maxima seen, including the central one, is
explanation: n ≤ d/λ = 2000/600 ≈ 3.3, so orders 1, 2 and 3 appear on each side of the central maximum, giving 2 × 3 + 1 = 7 maxima. The value 3 counts the highest order on one side only.

stem: A single-mode optical fibre differs from a multimode step-index fibre mainly because
options: its core is very narrow, so light follows almost one path
its cladding has a higher refractive index than the core
its core is made of plastic with a large diameter
light in it travels by refraction rather than reflection
explanation: A single-mode fibre has a core only a few micrometres across, so light travels essentially along one path and pulses do not spread by taking different routes; this suits long-distance links. In every fibre the cladding has the lower refractive index, otherwise total internal reflection could not occur.
